meta.description: An open source application built using the new router, server components and everything new in Next.js 13.

gist.one: A demo website where people sign in, write posts, subscribe and read docs.
gist.analogy: Think of it like a model home for web builders: fully furnished with login, payments, blog and docs, to show what modern Next.js can do.
gist.users: Developers studying how a real Next.js 13 app is built; its visitors write posts and pay for a Pro plan.
does: Sign in with GitHub or email link
Write and edit posts in a dashboard
Subscribe to a Pro plan with Stripe
Read a blog and guides written in MDX
Switch between light and dark mode

nodes.label: A visitor
nodes.does: Opens pages, signs in, writes posts
nodes.more: Everything starts with someone opening the site in their browser. They read public pages, log in, and use the dashboard. The browser is the 'client' that talks to the app's server.

nodes.label: The pages
nodes.does: Builds what you see on screen
nodes.more: Each folder under app/ is a web address. Marketing, docs, login, dashboard and editor pages live in separate groups, each with its own shared layout. Next.js calls these 'routes' and 'layouts', and many are server components that are built on the server before reaching you.

nodes.label: Building blocks
nodes.does: Buttons, menus, forms, dialogs
nodes.more: Reusable pieces such as buttons, dialogs and the post editor are shared across pages. They are styled with Tailwind classes and built on Radix UI for accessible behavior. In React these pieces are called components.

nodes.label: Docs and blog files
nodes.does: Holds articles written as text files
nodes.more: Blog posts, guides and pages are written as MDX files in a content folder. Contentlayer turns them into data the pages can read when the site is built. MDX is Markdown that can include React components.

nodes.label: The doors
nodes.does: Receive requests to save or change things
nodes.more: When you save a post or start a subscription, the browser sends a request to a URL under app/api. Each handler checks who you are, checks the data is valid with Zod, then does the work. These are called route handlers.

nodes.label: Login system
nodes.does: Knows who you are
nodes.more: Auth.js handles sign-in by GitHub or a magic email link and remembers you with a session token. The sign-in email is sent through Postmark. Handlers and pages ask it who is logged in before showing private things.

nodes.label: The database
nodes.does: Remembers users, posts and subscriptions
nodes.more: Users, sessions, posts and Stripe details are stored in a MySQL database. Prisma lets the code ask for data using simple functions instead of raw database language. That layer is called an ORM.

nodes.label: Stripe
nodes.does: Takes payments, reports back
nodes.more: Stripe hosts the payment page and handles the card. When a payment succeeds, Stripe calls the app's own address to say so, and the app updates the user's plan. That call-back is a webhook.

terms.plain: A page piece that is built on the server, so the browser just receives the finished result.
terms.like: A meal cooked in the kitchen, not at your table.

terms.plain: A small function that answers a request sent to a certain web address.
terms.like: A counter clerk who handles one kind of request.

terms.plain: A helper that lets code talk to a database using normal functions instead of database commands.
terms.like: A translator between you and the filing clerk.

terms.plain: A small proof that you are logged in, which the browser sends with every request.
Checking incoming data has the right shape before using it.
terms.like: A bouncer checking tickets at the door.

terms.plain: Another service calling your app's address to tell you something happened.
terms.like: A delivery driver ringing your doorbell.

layers.ui: Every page lives in `app/` grouped as marketing, docs, auth, dashboard and editor, using shared pieces in `components/` and `components/ui/`.
layers.logic: Helpers for login, Stripe, subscription checks, validation and class names live in `lib/`; `env.mjs` checks that required secrets exist.
layers.server: Request handlers under `app/api/` serve posts, users, Stripe and webhooks; `middleware.ts` runs before pages to guard private areas.
layers.data: `lib/db.ts` opens the Prisma connection and `prisma/migrations/` holds the SQL that built the MySQL tables.
layers.support: Settings in `package.json`, `tailwind.config.js` and `contentlayer.config.js`; `config/` has site and docs menus. There are no automated tests.

meta.description: 📊 Send TradingView alerts to Telegram, Discord, Slack, Twitter and Email.

gist.one: A small server that forwards TradingView trading alerts to your chat apps and email.
gist.analogy: Think of it like a mail sorter: one alert arrives at the door, and copies get sent to Telegram, Discord, Slack, Twitter and email.
gist.users: Traders who want price alerts pushed to their phone or team chat without watching charts.
does: Checks a secret key and sender address
Posts messages to Telegram, Discord, Slack
Turns channels on or off in config

nodes.label: TradingView
nodes.does: Spots a price move and sends an alert
nodes.more: You set a rule on a chart, like 'price crossed this line'. When it fires, TradingView sends a small message to a web address you chose. That kind of automatic message from one service to another is called a webhook.

nodes.label: The front door
nodes.does: Waits for alerts and checks them
nodes.more: This program stays running and listens at the /webhook address. It checks that the sender is really TradingView and that the secret key matches. The tool that makes this easy is Flask, a web framework.

nodes.label: Your settings
nodes.does: Holds keys, tokens and on/off switches
nodes.more: One file lists your secret key, which channels are turned on, and the passwords each service needs. Both the front door and the sender read from it. Keeping settings in one place is a common habit called a config file.

nodes.label: The sender
nodes.does: Copies the message to each enabled channel
nodes.more: It takes the alert text and goes through each channel in turn. For every channel that is switched on, it calls that service's helper library to deliver the message. A function that reacts to an incoming event like this is often called a handler.

nodes.label: Telegram
nodes.does: Delivers the message to a chat
nodes.more: The sender uses a Telegram bot token to post into a chat or channel. Telegram then pushes it to your phone.

nodes.label: Discord, Slack, X, email
nodes.does: Show the alert in other places
nodes.more: Discord and Slack accept messages posted to a special web address. Twitter uses the tweepy library, and email goes through a mail server using SMTP, the standard protocol for sending email.

terms.plain: A web address that one service calls automatically to tell another service something just happened.
terms.like: A doorbell that TradingView rings when your alert fires.

terms.plain: A Python toolkit that lets a program answer requests from the internet.
terms.like: A ready-made front desk for your program.

terms.plain: A simple text format for sending labeled information, like a key and a message.
terms.like: A form with labeled boxes, written as plain text.

terms.plain: A short list of internet addresses that are allowed in; everyone else is turned away.
terms.like: A guest list at the door.

terms.plain: A way to package a program with everything it needs so it runs the same anywhere.
terms.like: A lunchbox holding the meal and the cutlery.

layers.server: `main.py` listens for alerts at /webhook and checks them. `handler.py` sends the message out to each chat service.
layers.logic: `config.py` holds the secret key, on/off switches and login details for every channel. It acts as the settings brain the rest reads from.
layers.support: `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` package the bot for easy running, `requirements.txt` lists the libraries it needs, and `README.md` explains setup.

steps.md: The /webhook door receives the message and checks the sender's address is on the allowed list.
The secret key in the message is compared with the one saved here.
send_alert cleans up the text and checks which channels are switched on.
The bot posts the text into your Telegram chat, which pings your phone.
The request comes in and its secret key is read from the JSON.
The key does not match sec_key, so the check fails.
The server logs a refusal and replies 'Unauthorized' with code 401. Nothing is sent.

flask.why: The job is tiny: one address, one kind of request. Flask needs very little code for that, so the whole server fits in under 50 lines.

hot.title: Secrets are typed straight into a file
hot.md: Tokens, passwords and the secret key sit in plain text in the code. If this is pushed to GitHub they leak. Engineers use environment variables or a secrets manager instead.

hot.title: Sender check trusts a forgeable header
hot.md: The IP check reads X-Forwarded-For, which a caller can fake unless a trusted proxy sets it. An attacker could bypass the list, leaving only the key. Only trust that header behind your own proxy.

hot.title: Channels are sent one after another
hot.md: Each service is called in turn and waits for a reply. If Discord is slow, Telegram and email wait too, and TradingView may time out. Fix with background tasks or a queue.

hot.title: Repeated code and missing-field handling
hot.md: Each channel repeats the same try/except pattern, and a missing 'msg' field would crash the whole send. Pull the shared logic into small functions and validate input up front.

meta.description: Code for multiplayer snake game with socket.io tutorial

gist.one: A two-player Snake game you play live in your browser against a friend.
gist.analogy: Think of it like a shared game table: a referee in the middle moves the pieces, and both players just watch and send moves.
gist.users: Friends who want a quick head-to-head Snake match, and learners studying real-time multiplayer code.
does: Create a game and get a code
Join a friend's game by code
Steer your snake with arrow keys
Eat food and see live updates
Declare a winner when someone crashes

nodes.label: Two players
nodes.does: Press keys and watch the board
nodes.more: Each player opens the game page in a browser. They press arrow keys to steer and see the board redraw many times a second. In technical terms, each browser is a client.

nodes.label: Browser game page
nodes.does: Draws the board, sends key presses
nodes.more: This code listens for clicks and key presses, sends them to the server, and paints the snakes and food on a canvas. It never decides who wins; it only shows what it is told.

nodes.label: Live connection
nodes.does: Carries messages both ways instantly
nodes.more: Normal web pages only answer when you ask. Socket.IO keeps a phone-line-style connection open so the server can push updates to you any time. It is built on a technology called WebSockets.

nodes.label: Game server
nodes.does: Manages rooms and runs the clock
nodes.more: The server creates a game room with a short code, lets a second player join, and ticks a timer 10 times a second. Each tick it asks the game rules to move the snakes, then broadcasts the result.

nodes.label: Game rules
nodes.does: Moves snakes, spots crashes, places food
nodes.more: This is the referee. On each tick it moves every snake one step, checks for walls and food, and says who won. Repeating this update step over and over is called a game loop.

nodes.label: Server memory
nodes.does: Remembers each room's current game
nodes.more: Games are kept in plain variables while the server runs, not in a database. That makes it fast and simple, but everything vanishes if the server restarts.

terms.plain: The client is the player's browser, and the server is the central program that runs the actual game.
A tool that keeps a live two-way connection open between each browser and the server.
terms.like: A phone call instead of sending letters.

terms.plain: A named message, like 'keydown' or 'gameState', that one side sends and the other listens for.
terms.like: Ringing a specific doorbell so the right person answers.

terms.plain: A private group of connections that only hear each other, here the two players in one match.
terms.like: A private chat channel with a secret code.

terms.plain: Code that repeats on a timer: move things, check rules, send the result.
terms.like: A flipbook where each page is one tiny moment.

terms.plain: A blank rectangle on a web page where code can draw shapes.
terms.like: A whiteboard the code draws squares on.

layers.ui: The page players see: `frontend/index.html` holds the menu, code box and canvas, styled in the same file.
layers.server: `server/server.js` accepts connections, creates and joins rooms, and runs the timer; `server/utils.js` makes room codes and `server/constants.js` sets speed and grid size.
layers.support: Only `README.md`, which points to the YouTube tutorials. There are no tests or config files.

journeys.title: When you press New Game and steer

steps.md: You click the New Game button on the start screen.
The click handler tells the server 'newGame', then shows the canvas.
Socket.IO carries the message from your browser to the server instantly.
The server makes a 5-letter room code, creates a game, and sends the code back.
Each tick, the game loop moves both snakes and checks for crashes or food.
Your browser receives the new state and repaints the snakes and food.

journeys.title: When a friend joins with your code

steps.md: Friend types your code and clicks Join; the page sends 'joinGame' with it.
The server checks that the room exists and holds exactly one player.
The friend is added as player 2 and the game timer starts.
Snakes begin moving according to each player's key presses.

socketio.name: Socket.IO
socketio.role: Keeps live connections open and groups players into rooms.
socketio.why: A real-time game needs the server to push updates constantly. Socket.IO makes rooms, named events and reconnection easy, with less setup than raw WebSockets.

alts.name: ws (WebSockets)
alts.when: You want a lighter, lower-level library without extra features.

alts.name: Server-Sent Events
alts.when: The server only needs to push updates one way.

alts.name: Colyseus
alts.when: You want a full multiplayer game framework with built-in state sync.

lang.name: JavaScript
lang.why: The browser only runs JavaScript, and Node.js lets the server use the same language too. One language for both halves keeps a small game easy to follow.

alts.name: TypeScript
alts.when: You want the editor to catch mistakes in message shapes, at the cost of a build step.

alts.name: Python
alts.when: You prefer its syntax on the server, but the browser still needs JavaScript.

roles.server/game.js: The rules: creates the game, moves snakes, and finds a winner.

roles.frontend/index.html: The page layout: start menu, code input and the game canvas.

hot.title: Hard-coded for exactly two players
hot.md: The loop reads `players[0]` and `players[1]` directly, so adding a third player or a solo mode means rewriting it. An engineer would loop over a list of players instead.

hot.title: Wall check uses an off-by-one edge
hot.md: The checks use `> GRID_SIZE` rather than `>=`, so a snake can sit one square past the visible edge before losing. Comparing against the true last cell would fix it.

hot.title: Server address is hard-coded
hot.md: The page connects to one specific Heroku URL. If that app goes away, the game breaks for everyone. Reading the address from config or the page's own host is safer.

hot.title: Games live only in server memory
hot.md: All rooms sit in plain variables, so a restart wipes every match and a second server could not share them. A shared store like Redis would help.

hot.title: Uses an old Socket.IO room lookup
hot.md: `io.sockets.adapter.rooms[roomName]` follows an older Socket.IO style. Newer versions return a Map, so upgrading could break joining until the lookup code is updated.
